title: How to Pose for Photos: Simple Poses That Look Natural — cv.cm
description: How to pose for photos if you are not a model: posture, weight on the back leg, body angle, chin and hands, plus standing, sitting, walking and group poses.
h1: How do you pose for photos and look natural?
answer: Stand tall, put your weight on your back leg, and turn your body about 45 degrees from the camera with your face turned back. Push your chin slightly forward and down, keep a small gap between your arms and body, and give your hands something to do. Breathe out just before the shot, and move slightly between frames.

sections.h: Why poses look stiff, and the basic fix
body: Most people stand facing the camera square-on, arms pressed to their sides, weight on both feet, and hold their breath. The camera flattens the body, so this looks wide and tense. Photographers fix it with small changes that create angles and space.

ol: Posture: stand tall as if a string pulls the top of your head up. Relax the shoulders down.
Weight on the back leg: shift your weight to the leg farther from the camera and bend the front knee slightly. The hips tilt and one shoulder drops a little, which looks relaxed.
Body angle: turn the hips and shoulders about 45 degrees away from the camera, then turn your face back towards it.
Chin forward and down: push the face slightly forward, as if to look over a fence, then tilt it down a little. This defines the jawline and removes a double chin.
Arms off the body: leave a small gap between arm and waist. Pressed arms look wider.
Breathe out: exhale just before the shutter. The shoulders drop and the face relaxes.

body: The photographer can help too. A camera just above eye level is flattering for the face. For a full-length shot, a camera at about waist height keeps legs from looking short. A wide 0.5x lens close to someone makes whatever is nearest the camera look bigger.

sections.h: What to do with your hands
body: Hands are the most common problem. Without a task, they hang or clench. Give them one of these jobs:

ul: One hand in a pocket, thumb out, or just the thumb hooked in a pocket.
Hand on the hip with the elbow pointing back, not to the side.
Touching something: a wall, a railing, a chair back, your collar, an earring, your hair.
Holding something: a cup, a bag strap, flowers, a book, sunglasses, a jacket over the shoulder.
Arms loosely crossed, with fingers relaxed and visible.
Hands together in front at waist height, held lightly.

body: Show the side of the hand to the camera, not the flat back or the palm. Keep fingers slightly curved and relaxed. Touch lightly; if your knuckles turn white, you are gripping.

body: These poses work for most people and most places. Try three or four of them in one session and take several frames of each.

sections.h: Poses for men, women and everyone
body: There are no rules about who uses which pose. But some habits help people get the look they want.

ul: For a strong, solid look: stand with feet about shoulder width apart, shoulders square or slightly angled, hands in pockets or arms loosely crossed, chin level and forward. Leaning slightly towards the camera looks confident.
For a softer, slimmer look: weight on the back leg, front knee bent and turned in a little, body angled, arms away from the waist, a gentle head tilt.
Sitting: men often sit with knees apart and forearms on the thighs; women often turn both knees to one side. Both look better with a straight back and sitting on the front of the seat.
Older people and people with limited mobility: use a chair or a wall to lean on, and keep poses simple. A relaxed face matters more than the pose.

body: With two or more people, closeness is the main rule. Gaps between people look cold in a photo even when they feel normal in real life.

ul: Couples: stand close, turned slightly towards each other. Try a back hug, walking hand in hand, or foreheads touching.
Small groups: stagger heads at different heights. Some people stand, some sit, some lean. Avoid a straight row of heads at the same level.
Large groups: put taller people in the middle and back. Ask everyone to check they can see the camera with both eyes.
Focus and aperture: for one row use about f/4; for several rows use f/5.6 to f/8 so everyone is sharp. On a phone, avoid portrait mode for groups, because it can blur people in the back row.
Take many frames: with five or more people, someone will blink. Shoot a burst and choose the best, or combine faces later.

sections.h: How to look natural in front of the camera
body: Natural photos usually come from movement and attention, not from holding a pose.

ol: Do something: walk, turn, fix your jacket, look at the view, talk to the photographer.
Use the count: look away, and on three, look back at the lens. The first moment of eye contact looks fresh.
Smile with the eyes: think of a real person or memory. A held smile fades after a few seconds; reset by relaxing the face and smiling again.
Tongue behind the top teeth: a small trick that keeps a smile from looking forced.
Ask for burst: on a phone, hold or swipe the shutter button (depending on the phone) to take a burst, then pick the best frame.
Practise: look at your test shots on the screen and adjust. Five minutes of practice changes a lot.

body: If you are taking photos of yourself with a timer or a remote, see the self-portrait photography guide on this shelf. For photographers directing a sitter, the portrait photography tips guide covers light and lens choice.

faq.q: What is the most flattering pose for photos?
faq.a: The three-quarter stand: body turned about 45 degrees from the camera, weight on the back leg, face turned back to the camera, and chin slightly forward and down.

faq.q: How do I stop looking awkward in photos?
faq.a: Give your hands a task, keep moving slightly between frames, and breathe out just before the shot. Ask for several frames so you can pick a relaxed one.

faq.q: Which side is my good side for photos?
faq.a: Take two quick selfies in the same light, one with each side towards the camera, and compare. Many faces are slightly asymmetric, and most people prefer one side.

faq.q: How do I pose if I am not photogenic?
faq.a: Being photogenic is mostly practice and good light. Face soft light from a window or open shade, use the three-quarter angle, and look at your test shots to see what works for you.

faq.q: Should I look at the camera or away?
faq.a: Both. Eye contact looks direct and personal; looking away looks candid. Take a few of each, and look at the lens itself, not the screen.
